article.headline: Sci-Hub Adds an AI Layer to Its 88-Million-Paper Archive
article.lede: Alexandra Elbakyan's Sci-Hub — the world's best-known repository of academic papers obtained without publisher authorization — expanded its footprint in April 2026 by releasing Sci-Bot, an AI assistant that searches 88 million papers and generates answers with clickable citations. The tool's debut has reignited a long-running argument about who actually pays for science and who profits from distributing it.
article.body:
Sci-Bot, accessible at sci-bot.ru, is described by Sci-Hub as an AI that "does not hallucinate and churn out made-up references" because it draws only from papers in the existing Sci-Hub archive rather than from general training data. In practice, testers at *Chemical & Engineering News* found it performed well for established methods but thin on recent work — publishers have tightened defenses against Sci-Hub's harvesting, leaving gaps in the last few years of literature. Responses typically surface fewer than ten citations, which limits the tool's usefulness for systematic literature reviews.

The sarcastic framing of the viral post crystallizes a genuine structural grievance. A 2005 Deutsche Bank (DBK.DE) research report labeled academic publishing a **"bizarre triple-pay system"**: governments fund the research through grants, public universities pay the salaries of scientists who peer-review manuscripts without additional fee, and those same institutions then pay again to access the published result. That structure has since grown more elaborate: major journals now levy *article processing charges* (APCs) — fees of roughly $2,000 to $3,000 at leading publishers — to make papers freely available online, a model known as *gold open access*. Peer reviewers remain unpaid throughout. For a reader seeking a single paper, the typical purchase price on ScienceDirect, Elsevier's distribution platform, runs roughly $31 to $45.

**RELX Group** (REL.L), the Anglo-Dutch information conglomerate that owns Elsevier, reported £3.1 billion in revenue from its Scientific, Technical & Medical segment in 2024, at an adjusted operating margin of roughly 37 to 40 percent — comparable to the most profitable consumer technology businesses and well above the mid-teens to low-twenties margins of Elsevier's nearest rivals. The gap is not lost on the research community: in March 2025, four U.S. university researchers filed a federal antitrust lawsuit against Elsevier and five other major publishers, alleging they had colluded to extract unpaid peer-review labor and suppress competition among journals, calling the arrangement "remarkably profitable for the publisher defendants, while doing tremendous damage to science and the public interest."

Sci-Hub has attracted legal action across multiple jurisdictions since its founding in 2011. Elsevier won a $15 million default judgment against it in U.S. federal court in 2017, forcing a domain change. In August 2025, the Delhi High Court ordered Indian internet service providers to block Sci-Hub and all mirror sites, ruling that Elbakyan had violated a 2020 undertaking not to distribute newly copyrighted content. Sci-Bot — launched after that ruling — is not named in the injunction, though its legal standing in restrictive jurisdictions is untested. Elbakyan, who has lived in Russia since Sci-Hub's founding and was named one of *Nature*'s ten most influential scientists in 2016, grounds her work in Article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which affirms the right to participate in scientific advancement.

One researcher quoted by *Chemical & Engineering News* described the situation as "deeply ironic": Sci-Hub faces sustained multi-jurisdictional prosecution while major AI companies train on copyrighted academic text at scale with comparatively little judicial pushback. That asymmetry — unauthorized redistribution aggressively litigated, mass ingestion largely tolerated — may prove as consequential for the future of scholarly communication as the debate over APCs.

concepts.definition: A fee paid by an author — or their institution or funder — to a journal in order to make the published paper freely available online. APCs typically range from a few hundred dollars at smaller publishers to over $9,000 at top-tier journals such as those in the Nature portfolio. Because most research is grant-funded, the cost ultimately falls largely on public money.

A publishing model in which the final published version of an article is made freely available immediately upon publication via the journal's own website, usually funded by APCs paid by the author. Distinct from green open access, where authors self-archive a preprint or accepted manuscript in an institutional repository without paying the publisher.

A phrase coined in a 2005 Deutsche Bank research report describing the unusual economics of academic publishing: the state funds the underlying research, pays the salaries of scientists who peer-review manuscripts for free, and then purchases the published output through library subscriptions — effectively paying three times for the same intellectual work.

The process by which scientists evaluate each other's manuscripts before publication, assessing methodology, originality, and accuracy. Reviewers are almost universally unpaid by publishers, treating it as a professional obligation. The aggregate value of this labor has been estimated at over $1.5 billion annually in the United States alone.

A structured, comprehensive search and synthesis of all published research on a defined question, using explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria. Distinct from a narrative review, it aims to minimize selection bias and is the gold standard for evidence-based medicine and policy — and requires broad, reproducible coverage of the literature rather than a handful of citations.

article.fact_check: The tweet claims authors pay "$3,000 to publish" and readers pay "$40 per article." Both are approximately right but imprecise. The U.S. average APC is roughly $2,177 according to NIH analysis; $3,000 is more typical of major Elsevier and hybrid journals but is not universal across all publishers. The per-article purchase price on ScienceDirect runs approximately $31 to $45, so "$40" is a reasonable shorthand. The tweet cites "85+ million papers"; Sci-Hub's own count as of July 2022 was 88.3 million, making the claim conservative rather than inflated. None of these discrepancies undermine the core argument.
